{"statements": {"L6.1": {"established": "yes", "quote": "Choose the unique $n$ for which
\[
 a_n<x\le a_{n+1}.
\]
Since $x\in S$, it has gcd greater than $1$ with each of $a_1,\ldots,a_n$. The minimality in the definition of $a_{n+1}$ therefore gives $a_{n+1}\le x$. Hence $x=a_{n+1}$.", "note": "Correct characterization: terms are exactly elements of S that are >= a_1."}, "L6.2": {"established": "no", "quote": null, "note": "Replaced by a false lemma: pairwise-intersecting families need not have finitely many minimal transversals; induction step ignores 'meets C' hypothesis."}, "L6.3": {"established": "partial", "quote": "Membership in $S$ depends only on the residue class modulo $L$, because each $b_j$ divides $L$. Let $T$ be the number of residue classes modulo $L$ which belong to $S$.", "note": "Counting/assembly from n=1 written correctly, but rests entirely on the false finiteness lemma producing b_1..b_s."}}, "S_ref": 0, "notes": "The write-up nails the characterization and the mod-L counting assembly, but its finiteness input is the false claim that any pairwise-intersecting family has finitely many minimal transversals (ledger counterexample F_k). The induction wrongly assumes every transversal meets C when passing to F_c. No large-prime erasure argument appears."}
